# SK2192 — `==` on spans compares memory locations

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`==` or `!=` binds to `Span<T>`'s or `ReadOnlySpan<T>`'s operator, which is true only when both spans point at the same memory and length.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

The operator reads like string equality and answers a question about addresses. Two spans over identical text compare `false`, and the same span compared with itself compares `true`, so the shape passes whatever test was written for it first and fails on the data. ⚠ **`span == "abc"` is the case that misleads hardest**: the implicit conversion from `string` makes it look like ordinary text comparison and it is a memory comparison against a freshly made span over the literal, which can never be equal.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static bool IsYes(System.ReadOnlySpan<char> value) => value == "yes";
```

Write:

```csharp
static bool IsYes(System.ReadOnlySpan<char> value) => value.SequenceEqual("yes");
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **It compiles, and the brief that carried this rule said it does not.** Measured on a probe built outside this repository: `ReadOnlySpan<char> == ReadOnlySpan<char>`, `Span<char> == Span<char>`, `ReadOnlySpan<byte> == ReadOnlySpan<byte>` and `ReadOnlySpan<char> == string` all build clean at `net10.0`, with no compiler warning and nothing from the .NET analyzers at `AnalysisMode=All` — the span types carry their own `operator ==`. ⚠ **What does *not* compile is `span.Equals(span)`**: `CS1503`, because the only `Equals` in reach takes `object` and a span cannot be boxed. So "`.Equals` where `SequenceEqual` was meant" is not a shape that exists on spans, and the operator is the whole rule. The test is on the **bound operator method**, so a type that merely holds a span is never reported. ⚠ **`default` and `null` operands are excluded**: `span == default` is the idiomatic "is this the default span" test and is asking about memory deliberately. ⚠ **The replacement is bound before it is offered, not merely composed.** `SequenceEqual` is an extension on `System.MemoryExtensions`, so a file without `using System;` would get text that parses and does not compile, and the element type has to satisfy the overload in reach. Speculative binding at the comparison's own position is what decides; where it does not bind there is no finding rather than a fix that breaks the build. That also means an element type with no usable `SequenceEqual` overload is silently declined. `fixIsSafe: false`, for the reason `SK2040` gives about the same kind of edit: the fix changes the answer, and changing the answer is the entire point of the finding.
